evidence.role: Direct retrieval is grounded in the verified Lesson 8 handoff

hints: Divide the absolute uncertainty by the measured value.
Convert the resulting fraction to a percentage.

walkthrough.text: The measured value is 15.0 cm and the absolute uncertainty is 0.6 cm.
Fractional uncertainty = 0.6 cm / 15.0 cm = 0.040; the centimetre units cancel.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.040 × 100 percent = 4.0 percent.
Independent check: 4.0 percent of 15.0 cm is 0.60 cm, matching the stated absolute uncertainty.

ai_rubric.observable: Divides the absolute uncertainty 0.6 cm by the measured value 15.0 cm and multiplies by 100 percent
Obtains a percentage uncertainty of 4.0 percent

evidence.role: Directly grounds the two controlled definitions

hints: Identify what is needed to specify the size of each type completely.
Only one of the two types also needs direction.

walkthrough.text: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude only.
A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction.
The distinguishing property is direction: it is required for a vector but not for a scalar.

ai_rubric.observable: States that a scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude only
States that a vector quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction

evidence.role: Grounds classification of mixed familiar quantities including force and momentum

hints: Test each quantity in a pair separately.
Ask whether its complete specification requires direction.

walkthrough.text: Force requires a magnitude and direction, so force is vector.
Momentum also requires a magnitude and direction, so momentum is vector.
Every other option contains at least one scalar. Therefore select A.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects force and momentum as two vector quantities

evidence.role: The mapped example demand and its whole-question context ground direction as the distinguishing vector property

hints: Recall which type includes direction in its specification.
Decide whether reversing only direction changes that specification.

walkthrough.text: A scalar quantity has magnitude only, so reversing a direction that is not part of it does not change the scalar.
A vector quantity includes direction, so reversing direction changes the vector even when its magnitude is fixed.
Select B.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects that reversing direction leaves a scalar unchanged but changes a vector

evidence.role: Grounds classification from complete and incomplete physical-quantity descriptions

hints: First classify each named physical quantity.
A vector record needs one item beyond magnitude and unit.

walkthrough.text: Temperature and speed are scalars, so their magnitude and unit are enough.
Force is vector, and option D includes its direction east.
Displacement is vector, but option C gives no direction. It is incomplete, so select C.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies displacement = 8.0 m as incomplete because displacement also requires a direction

evidence.role: Grounds classification of several syllabus quantities and comparison of properties shared by both categories

hints: Classify each readout by whether direction is required for complete specification.
For the final part, name properties found in both categories rather than the property that separates them.

walkthrough.text: Sort the three quantities fully described by magnitude and unit: time, speed and energy are scalars.
Sort the three quantities that also require direction: acceleration, force and momentum are vectors.
Both categories describe physical quantities, so both have magnitude and an appropriate unit. Direction is not shared.

evidence.role: Grounds scalar classification in mixed lists

hints: Ask whether any of these three quantities points in a physical direction.
A context involving motion does not make every reported quantity vector.

walkthrough.text: Time is scalar because a duration has magnitude only.
Speed is scalar because it states how fast without specifying a direction.
Energy is scalar because its value has no direction.

ai_rubric.observable: Classifies time as a scalar quantity
Classifies speed as a scalar quantity
Classifies energy as a scalar quantity

evidence.role: Grounds vector classification of acceleration, force and momentum

hints: Check whether reversing the stated direction would change each physical quantity.
The arrows or compass words are part of each complete readout.

walkthrough.text: Acceleration is vector because it requires direction as well as magnitude.
Force is vector because equal forces in opposite directions are physically different.
Momentum is vector because its complete specification includes a direction.

ai_rubric.observable: Classifies acceleration as a vector quantity
Classifies force as a vector quantity
Classifies momentum as a vector quantity

evidence.role: Whole-question context grounds properties shared by scalar and vector physical quantities

hints: Look at what is recorded for every physical quantity on the panel.
Do not use direction because it is not shared by scalars.

walkthrough.text: Every listed physical quantity has a numerical size, called its magnitude.
Every listed physical quantity is expressed with an appropriate unit.
Therefore the two shared properties are magnitude and unit.

ai_rubric.observable: States that both scalar and vector physical quantities have magnitude
States that both scalar and vector physical quantities have an appropriate unit

evidence.role: Grounds classification and valid examples; earlier Module 1 supplies the magnitude-and-unit reporting contract

hints: First classify each named quantity by its physical meaning.
Then check whether every record contains the information required by that category.

walkthrough.text: Use earlier learning to check that every record includes a numerical magnitude and unit.
Classify mass and time as scalars, and force and velocity as vectors.
The force record lacks direction, while the velocity record includes west.
A direction word cannot change mass into a vector because direction is not part of the physical meaning of mass.

evidence.role: Grounds classification and production of valid scalar and vector examples

hints: Ask whether each quantity requires direction in addition to magnitude and unit.
Classify the quantity itself, not the completeness of its record.

walkthrough.text: Mass is scalar because it has magnitude only.
Force is vector because it requires direction.
Time is scalar because a duration does not have direction.
Velocity is vector because west is part of its complete specification.

Classifies force as a vector quantity
Classifies time as a scalar quantity
Classifies velocity as a vector quantity

evidence.role: Grounds applying definitions to judge whether a physical-quantity record is complete

hints: Magnitude and unit are already present in every record.
Check the records belonging to vector quantities for one additional property.

walkthrough.text: The force record has magnitude 6.0 and unit N, but force is vector.
A direction is therefore required to specify the force completely.
The velocity record is already complete because it includes the direction west.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies force = 6.0 N as the incomplete record
States that the direction of the force is the extra information required

evidence.role: Grounds reasoning from the controlled scalar definition rather than from an attached label

hints: Decide whether direction is part of the physical meaning of mass.
An added word does not change the defining properties of a quantity.

walkthrough.text: Mass is fully specified by its magnitude and unit.
Mass has no physical direction, so an attached compass word would be unrelated to the mass itself.
Therefore adding a direction word cannot turn mass into a vector quantity.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that mass has no physical direction and is fully specified by magnitude and unit, so adding a direction word does not make it a vector
